summary: No orders: the S&P 500 fund ended Tuesday further below its 200-day average and futures point to a fall of about 2% this morning, so the buy-back signal is still days away; the cash waits for that signal or 10 December at the latest, and the health care fund stays because it is well above its sell line.
thesis:
Where the account stands. At the end of Tuesday 24 November it was worth $972.72 against $946.00 for the benchmark, $1,000 left in an S&P 500 fund. The gap widened again to about $27 because the market slipped while the account sat mostly in cash and the health care fund rose. Ten trading days is still far too short to call this skill or luck.

What has happened since the last decision:

- Tuesday gave back part of Monday's rebound. The S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq Composite 1.5%, while the Dow rose 0.9% on strong results from retailers. Chip stocks fell about 8% and the semiconductor fund SMH 7.3%. Quieter areas did well: health care (XLV) rose 3.0%, consumer staples (XLP) 1.7% and real estate (XLRE) 1.3%.
- This morning, before the open, futures point clearly lower: the S&P 500 about 2% down, the Nasdaq 100 close to 3% down and the Dow about 1.3% down. Chip makers in Asia fell sharply overnight and Nvidia is about 5% lower before the open. Reuters reported that the administration is preparing new tariffs on about 16 trading partners, including China and the EU; the timing and rates are not confirmed. The market's fear gauge, the VIX, is near 31.
- October PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred measure, comes out at 8:30 a.m. New York time, after this decision is written. Forecasts are 0.3% for the month and about 3.2% over the year for the core measure. Traders put the chance of a quarter-point rate increase on 9 December at about 97% to 98%. The 10-year Treasury yield is about 4.90%. Markets are closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it:

1. XLV: keep. It ended Tuesday at $184.72, about 5% above the $176 sell line and above its 50-day average ($177.08). I found no new report widening the Medicare proposal that was named as the other reason to sell. It is now about 3% below what I paid. It has done its job of holding up while the market falls, and it is the account's only holding in a sector that is rising. Selling it now would mean paying fees to hold more cash on a day the market is expected to drop. If it ends any day below $176, the next decision sells it.

2. Cash, about $827 (85%). The plan buys back the S&P 500 fund SPY when it ends two trading days in a row at least 1% above its 200-day average. That average is $733.04, so the line is about $740.37. SPY ended Tuesday at $718.78, about 1.9% below the average and about 2.9% below the line, and futures point to a further fall of about 2% today. With Thursday closed, the earliest the signal could come is the end of Monday 30 November, and that would need a rise of more than 5% from this morning's expected level. So I wait. The written end date stands: the account goes back to being fully invested no later than 10 December, the first trading day after the Fed decision, whether or not the signal comes.

I looked again at other uses for the cash. Consumer staples (XLP) is above all its averages and has risen 5.4% in 20 days, but a short stay before 10 December would cost about 0.3% in fees with no specific, checkable reason beyond momentum, and the plan says to trade rarely. Treasury bills (SGOV) would earn less than the fees over two weeks. Longer bond funds (IEF, TLT) rose last week but could fall if today's inflation figure is hot. Chip and technology funds are far below their averages and still falling; buying them would be guessing at a bottom. None of these meets the plan's bar today.

This is not the first decision of the month, so there is no monthly review. The first is due at the start of December.
risks: If the market turns up sharply after a soft inflation figure, the account will miss the rebound and may buy back above the price at which SPY was sold. If it keeps falling, the 10 December date could put the cash back in at a bad moment. New tariffs or a hot PCE reading could hit health care along with the rest of the market and push XLV toward its $176 line. Before-the-open futures can change by 9:30, and figures differ somewhat between sources taken at different times.
